articles.title: Global consumption-based deforestation carbon emissions and regional hotspots: 2001–2020
articles.titleEn: Global consumption-based deforestation carbon emissions and regional hotspots: 2001–2020
articles.abstract: The consumption-based carbon emissions dataset for deforestation provides an important perspective for developing effective emission mitigation policies. However, existing datasets are largely limited to national-scale and lack spatially explicit, high-resolution data at the global level. Here, we present a global, gridded dataset of consumption-based deforestation carbon emissions at 1 km resolution for 2001–2020. The dataset integrates spatial information on road networks, deforestation, and forest carbon fluxes with country-level global trade statistics. Our dataset shows that trade-related deforestation emissions amount to 39.6 Gt CO 2 e, constituting 31.8 % of global deforestation emissions. This new dataset fills a critical gap in spatially explicit consumption-based deforestation emissions data, and supports the development of targeted mitigation strategies from the consumer perspective. It also provides a valuable input for climate and carbon cycle models to assess the contribution of consumption-driven deforestation to global warming. Datasets are available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.28091879 (Tang et al., 2024).

articles.title: Global gridded air-sea oxygen flux inferred from a machine learning-based dissolved oxygen product
articles.titleEn: Global gridded air-sea oxygen flux inferred from a machine learning-based dissolved oxygen product
articles.abstract: We present estimates of the monthly open ocean air-sea O 2 flux from 2004 to 2024 on a 1 ° ×1° grid spanning 64.5° S to 79.5° N. The flux is computed using 4-dimensional ocean dissolved oxygen (DO) fields derived from Argo float and shipboard observations via machine learning algorithms (GOBAI-O 2 , Sharp et al., 2023). Flux uncertainties are quantified by generating a large ensemble of flux estimates, first propagating errors from the dissolved oxygen product, then computing fluxes across all combinations of three gas exchange parameterizations that account for bubble-mediated flux and three wind products. We apply DO adjustments to align our resolved global annual mean fluxes with those derived from scaling global ocean heat uptake and regional annual mean fluxes with those derived from ocean inversions. Our results show larger seasonal flux variations at high latitudes than at low latitudes, with clear differences between major ocean basins. Both adjusted and unadjusted annual mean flux estimates exhibit strong ocean O 2 sinks at high latitudes, weak sources in the low-to-mid latitude subtropics, and weak sinks near the Equator. The annual mean adjustment enhances ocean O 2 uptake in the northern high latitudes and reduces outgassing in the tropics and northern subtropics, while slightly weakening uptake in the Southern Ocean. We evaluate our flux seasonal cycles and annual mean values by comparing forward transport simulations with atmospheric O 2 observations from global airborne surveys and surface sampling stations. The simulations reproduce the observed mean seasonal cycles well, but some differences remain in the annual mean latitudinal gradients. We analyze fractional variance contributions from DO, wind, and gas exchange scheme uncertainties and their interactions at regional and hemispheric scales for both climatological monthly and annual mean fluxes. This dataset marks a major improvement over existing air-sea O 2 flux products, as it includes the resolution of interannual variability in the flux seasonal cycle, the use of advanced machine learning-based DO fields that better represent complex spatial and temporal patterns, and robust uncertainty quantification across various scales. This dataset is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22119163 (Jin, 2026).

articles.title: Ecological change in the native Scottish pinewoods since 1971 – data from the Bunce 2018–2022 re-survey
articles.titleEn: Ecological change in the native Scottish pinewoods since 1971 – data from the Bunce 2018–2022 re-survey
articles.abstract: The native pinewoods of Scotland are acknowledged to be an important ecological resource, both for their biodiversity value and as a cultural and amenity resource. Due to the unique nature of the habitat and its limited range, it plays a critical role as an early warning system for broader environmental issues. In the late 1960s and 70s, increased concern was expressed regarding a decline in the status and management of the pinewoods. In response to the concerns, an ecological monitoring survey was initiated by R. G. H. Bunce of the Nature Conservancy in 1971, recording ground flora, tree information, soils and other descriptive attributes. Since that time, interest in the pinewoods has increased further, and there is a general consensus that the habitat is more vulnerable than ever. Thanks to a recent repeat survey between 2018 and 2022, questions addressing the threats and changes occurring in the pinewoods can now be explored in a statistically robust way. These questions include issues surrounding the impacts of deer grazing, regeneration, the balance between native and exotic species, local disturbances, trends in ground flora species occurrences, climate change and recovery from acidification. The new data from the 2018–2022 survey are now publicly available via the following DOI: https://doi.org/10.5285/5e268e86-4a4f-4112-bf2d-c3b0179c915c (Smart et al., 2023). Change data are available at: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.34574874 (Wood et al., 2026).
articles.abstractEn: The native pinewoods of Scotland are acknowledged to be an important ecological resource, both for their biodiversity value and as a cultural and amenity resource. Due to the unique nature of the habitat and its limited range, it plays a critical role as an early warning system for broader environmental issues. In the late 1960s and 70s, increased concern was expressed regarding a decline in the status and management of the pinewoods. In response to the concerns, an ecological monitoring survey was initiated by R. G. H. Bunce of the Nature Conservancy in 1971, recording ground flora, tree information, soils and other descriptive attributes. articles.title: ALPAKAS: Alpine hydrographs and catchment attributes for karst springs
articles.titleEn: ALPAKAS: Alpine hydrographs and catchment attributes for karst springs
articles.abstract: Approximately 40 % of the European Alps consist of karstifiable rock. Due to their distinct recharge, storage, and discharge properties, karst aquifers are key components of the hydrological cycle and water supply in the Alpine region. However, large-sample datasets enabling comparative and data-driven analyses of karst spring discharge are currently lacking. Here, we present ALPAKAS (ALPine hydrographs and catchment Attributes for KArst Springs), the first large-sample benchmark dataset specifically dedicated to karst springs. ALPAKAS comprises 242 daily and 182 hourly quality-controlled and consistently preprocessed discharge time series from karst spring stations distributed across the EU Strategy for the Alpine Region (EUSALP) area, with stations located in seven countries. The dataset is complemented by both existing catchment delineations and circular catchment approximations, catchment-aggregated meteorological time series at multiple spatial scales, and a comprehensive set of static catchment attributes describing topography, positioning, meteorology, land cover, soil properties, and hydrogeology. In addition, the dataset includes karst-specific indices directly derived from the karst spring hydrographs. ALPAKAS is available via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19329693 (Joger et al., 2026) under an open-access licence and is accompanied by comprehensive documentation. By providing a harmonized, large-sample compilation of karst spring catchments across diverse Alpine settings, the dataset enables comparative analyses, model benchmarking, and robust assessments of hydrogeological processes and climate change impacts.

articles.title: Lake hydrochemistry and aquatic plant diversity across permafrost landscapes of Yakutia, Eastern Siberia
articles.titleEn: Lake hydrochemistry and aquatic plant diversity across permafrost landscapes of Yakutia, Eastern Siberia
articles.abstract: Central Yakutia in eastern Siberia is characterized by abundant lakes in permafrost-thaw depressions, named alaas. They constitute the traditional cultural landscape that is home to the indigenous Sakha people, providing critical ecosystem services. This study aims at assessing present-day lake characteristics and exploring their drivers based on lake hydrochemistry and aquatic and terrestrial plant diversity derived from sedimentary DNA in surface sediments. Macrophyte diversity reflects different lake types distinguished using both lake morphology and hydrochemistry. It also reveals a dominance of brackish water-tolerant cosmopolitan submerged macrophytes across all lakes, particularly Stuckenia and Potamogeton . In contrast, Myriophyllum and M. verticillatum are exclusively found in mountain lakes and freshwater lakes in the lowlands. The hydrochemical analysis reveals a clear distinction between low-mineralised mountain lakes and the highly variable hydrochemistry of the lowland lakes with much higher mineral content. Mountain lake hydrochemistry seems to be mainly determined by climate, whereas environmental drivers of hydrochemistry in lowland thermokarst lakes are more diverse. New thermokarst lakes are characterised by high dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and mainly located in forests. In contrast, connected alaas lakes, typically located in large alaas systems with settlements and active land use, display lower DOC and mineralisation, despite their location close to anthropogenic influence. We assume that temporary high discharge, such as during snowmelts, enables dilution, thus lowering organic and mineral contents. Future warming may lead to prolonged exposure to evaporation, but also to increased hydrological connectivity and increase in the number of connected alaas lakes, thereby potentially providing more freshwater to the region.

articles.title: Disentangling the biotic and abiotic drivers of evapotranspiration in a degraded raised bog
articles.titleEn: Disentangling the biotic and abiotic drivers of evapotranspiration in a degraded raised bog
articles.abstract: Despite covering only approximately 3 % of the Earth's land surface, peatlands are recognized as a key nature-based solution for climate change mitigation due to their substantial carbon storage and high potential for restoration. Beyond carbon sequestration, peatlands also influence the local climate through land–atmosphere energy exchange, with one of their key cooling mechanisms being the regulation of latent heat fluxes ( L E ). However, the interaction between abiotic (e.g., atmospheric and soil meteorological conditions) and biotic (e.g., canopy conductance ( g c ), gross primary productivity (GPP)) drivers on L E remains insufficiently understood, particularly in the context of drained peatlands dominated by heath and dwarf-shrub vegetation. Here, we analyzed eddy covariance measurements collected over three years between 2023 and 2025 at a drained raised bog in northwest Germany. Using high frequency CO 2 , H 2 O, energy flux, and meteorological measurements we (1) explored the daily and seasonal dynamics of L E , (2) quantified the influence of biotic and abiotic drivers on L E , and (3) determined the vegetation physiological thresholds at which g c limits L E due to an increase in atmospheric and soil dryness. To disentangle the biotic and abiotic controls of L E , we derived a continuous time series of g c by inverting the Penman-Monteith equation using 30 min L E fluxes measured with the eddy covariance method. This approach enabled us to estimate subdaily g c alongside GPP and continuous daily meteorological variables, including net radiation ( R n ), air temperature ( T a ), vapor pressure deficit (VPD, i.e., atmospheric dryness), groundwater table depth (WTD), and soil water content (SWC, i.e., soil dryness). Using daily mean data, detrending of mean seasonality, and removal of time lag, the variable component of the drivers was extracted and the effect size on L E was determined. R n and GPP showed the largest effect on L E , with marked differences in their effect during the growing season versus the non-growing season. During the growing season, R n and GPP have the largest effect on L E , while outside the growing season, WTD and VPD have the greatest impact. g c responded strongly to VPD but not to SWC. The peak of a local polynomial regression indicated the thresholds for VPD and SWC at which L E was limited by vegetation physiological responses ( g c ). With increase in atmospheric dryness, g c significantly limited L E above a VPD threshold of 7.6 hPa. These results help us better understand the potential impacts of environmental conditions on the evaporative cooling capacity of drained peatlands. Further research is needed to understand how occurrence of extreme climatic conditions will affect the relationships identified in this study.

articles.title: Present and future trends of extreme short-term rainfall events in Germany, by downscaling convective environments of ERA5 and a CMIP6 ensemble
articles.titleEn: Present and future trends of extreme short-term rainfall events in Germany, by downscaling convective environments of ERA5 and a CMIP6 ensemble
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: For the four main quadrant regions of Germany we study the possibility of projecting the occurrence of extreme convective rainfall events, as monitored by the CatRaRE database, into the future, based on CMIP6 projections of corresponding convective environments. We characterize such environments by using the atmospheric profile derivates convective available potential energy ( cape ) and convective inhibition ( cin ), along with model-simulated convective precipitation ( cp ). The convective environments are linked to the small-scale CatRaRE events by classifying the corresponding ERA5 fields according to the concurrent occurrence of such events. Classifiers are conventional machine-learning procedures along with more modern deep learning schemes. Positive centennial trends are identified for both antagonists cape and cin , serving as a source for large uncertainties of the corresponding CatRaRE-type trends. Their full distribution is analyzed using ANOVA, based on the factors of event severity, greenhouse gas emissions, climate models, classifiers, and region. Beyond all uncertainty, positive trends outweigh the negative ones for all regions.

articles.title: Partially functional hypomorphic missense variants in BRCA2 are reduced penetrance pathogenic variants
articles.titleEn: Partially functional hypomorphic missense variants in BRCA2 are reduced penetrance pathogenic variants
articles.abstract: Identification of partial loss-of-function (hypomorphic), reduced penetrance pathogenic missense variants (RPPVs) and assessment of the clinical relevance of these variants is needed for improved hereditary cancer risk estimation. Here we show that 70 candidate hypomorphic missense variants in the DNA-binding domain of BRCA2 reduce homologous recombination DNA repair activity and endogenous cell survival, decrease RAD51 foci formation, and increase sensitivity to Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors. The 34 “strong” hypomorphs with greatest effects on function are associated with moderate risks of female breast cancer and later ages of diagnosis than pathogenic variants (PVs), and 14 of these variants can be classified as “likely pathogenic” by integration of functional data into a ClinGen BRCA1/2 variant curation model. In addition, 32% of tumors with hypomorphic variants and corresponding loss of heterozygosity for BRCA2 display homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) compared to 83% of tumors with PVs and 7% with benign variants. These RPPVs represent a class of BRCA2 variants that have implications for the clinical management of carriers.

articles.title: Data‐Driven Flux Parameterization for the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
articles.titleEn: Data‐Driven Flux Parameterization for the Atmospheric Boundary Layer
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Turbulent fluxes in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) govern the exchange of momentum, heat, and mass between the surface and the atmosphere, thereby shaping the vertical structure of the ABL and influencing a wide range of engineering applications, atmospheric processes, and boundary layer dynamics. Accurate parameterization of these fluxes in coarse‐resolution weather and climate models remains challenging, particularly under unstable conditions where flux transport is strongly nonlocal and under stable conditions where turbulence may become intermittent and partially decoupled from surface forcing. In this study, we develop a data‐driven parameterization of turbulent fluxes using a novel formulation in which nondimensional fluxes are represented as a linearized convolution operation acting on the relevant nondimensional mean‐state profiles. A comprehensive high‐resolution large eddy simulation (LES) data set is generated for idealized flow over homogeneous surfaces across a range of stability conditions. Using selected training cases from this data set, we derive and test several first‐order versions of this linearized convolution flux parameterization, each based on different combinations of inputs, that map mean temperature and velocity profiles to heat and momentum fluxes. The best‐performing parameterization is determined as the one that minimizes the mean squared error in both training cases and unseen testing cases. The results indicate that the proposed method improves predictive skill relative to commonly used closures (the standard K‐profile parameterization is used here as the benchmark) while preserving a transparent operator structure that can be inspected for physical meaning. Rather than treating the learned closure as a purely empirical mapping, the present framework learns flux–profile relationships as operators constrained by the governing column dynamics, enabling the inferred operator kernels to reveal the spatial organization and locality or nonlocality of turbulent transport across stability regimes. Despite being restricted to linear operators, the resulting parameterization remains interpretable, performs strongly across diverse stability conditions, and tests successfully in a posteriori single column model simulations, yielding state profiles that agree closely with the LES data.

articles.title: Plain Urban Water Networks: Percolation Theory as a Tool for Bottleneck Identification and Connectivity Enhancement
articles.titleEn: Plain Urban Water Networks: Percolation Theory as a Tool for Bottleneck Identification and Connectivity Enhancement
articles.abstract: Plain urban water networks generally exhibit weak hydrodynamic conditions and limited hydraulic connectivity, resulting in multiple challenges related to flooding, water quality, and aquatic ecosystems. A favorable spatiotemporal hydrodynamic regime is essential for water networks to enhance connectivity and maintain their functional performance. Quickly identifying hydrodynamically weak bottleneck segments can support targeted improvement of the hydrodynamic regime of water networks. However, traditional scenario enumeration and scheme comparison are time‐consuming and provide limited guidance on which segments should be prioritized for improvement. This study presents a framework for identifying and prioritizing hydrodynamic bottleneck segments in water networks based on percolation theory. By integrating one‐dimensional hydrodynamic simulation with graph models, functional states (functional/non‐functional) are mapped into segments based on flow velocity thresholds, with segments below the thresholds classified as non‐functional. Bottleneck segments that most strongly control velocity‐based connectivity are then identified by tracking the critical transition threshold of the largest connected component. Improving the identified bottleneck segment enhanced network connectivity more than improving a segment with high betweenness centrality. As the bottleneck shifts to other segments once the original bottleneck is sufficiently improved, a cascading bottleneck prioritization method is proposed to update the bottleneck sequence and guide phased improvements. This approach provides a quantitative basis for progressively strengthening velocity‐based network connectivity. Comparative hydrodynamic modeling experiments supported the hydraulic consistency of bottleneck identification and improvement, while increasing computational efficiency by 70.6 times. Experiments on random geometric graphs further showed that water networks with similar structural degree patterns can exhibit comparable percolation behavior.

articles.title: Testing the temporal and spatial transferability of a water balance model using a parameter learning approach
articles.titleEn: Testing the temporal and spatial transferability of a water balance model using a parameter learning approach
articles.abstract: Reliable transferability of hydrological model parameters across time and space remains a challenge for large-scale water resources assessment. In this study, we investigate whether a differentiable hybrid framework can identify robust and physically coherent parameter sets for annual streamflow modeling across a large-sample dataset of 3044 catchments from eight countries. To focus on temporal and spatial transferability analysis, we work at the annual time scale using what we consider to be the simplest possible model: an annual anomaly model of climate elasticities, coupled with the Turc–Mezentsev formulation for the long-term streamflow mean (MQ). A dense neural network is trained in an end-to-end fashion to map catchment descriptors to the four model parameters: because the anomaly-model equations are fully differentiable with respect to their parameters, the gradients of the streamflow loss are backpropagated through these equations to the neural network weights. We evaluate the framework using three cross-validation settings inspired by Klemeš (1986): temporal, spatial, and combined temporal–spatial cross-validation. As a benchmark, we compare the hybrid model against local, catchment-by-catchment linear regressions under temporal cross-validation. Our results show that, for temporal transferability, our parameter learning approach outperforms local calibration, yielding higher Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values while producing elasticity coefficients that remain within plausible physical ranges, despite lacking explicit parameter constraints. By contrast, spatial transferability reveals a marked limitation: the anomaly component extrapolates well spatially, but regionalizing MQ from descriptors proves difficult, with MQ errors dominating the loss of performance in spatial and spatiotemporal cross-validation. Experiments with random descriptors further show that our parameter learning uses attributes mainly as catchment identifiers in temporal cross-validation but relies on their physical content to sustain spatial transfer, particularly for MQ. Overall, the study demonstrates that simple differentiable hybrid annual models can learn robust and interpretable anomaly parameters, while highlighting MQ regionalization as the main remaining bottleneck for spatially transferable annual streamflow predictions.

articles.title: Covariance-informed spatiotemporal clustering improves the detection of hazardous weather events
articles.titleEn: Covariance-informed spatiotemporal clustering improves the detection of hazardous weather events
articles.abstract: Spatiotemporal clustering can be used to detect weather events in multi-dimensional datasets. This method requires that the resolution of a dataset equivalently resolves variability across space and time, thereby normalizing the dataset for unbiased clustering across three dimensions. While spatiotemporal clustering is widely used, few studies quantitatively assess whether a dataset's resolution satisfies the normalization assumption required for unbiased clustering. To address this methodological gap, we present a framework to quantify the relationship between space and time using space time separable covariance modelling. We demonstrate that by defining a temporal resolution of interest (e.g., hours, days), the equivalent spatial resolution can be empirically derived using a space time metric. We present a case study using the unsupervised machine learning method Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN) to detect extreme heat and precipitation events across the Southeastern United States between 1940 and 2023 from ECMWF Reanalysis version 5 (ERA5) data. We analyse the behaviour of space time metrics for precipitation and heat index before selecting representative values. articles.title: EGGS-WG: an open source global gridded stochastic weather generator derived from ERA5-Land
articles.titleEn: EGGS-WG: an open source global gridded stochastic weather generator derived from ERA5-Land
articles.abstract: A new open source and freely available stochastic weather generator, the ERA5-land Global Gridded Stochastic Weather Generator (EGGS-WG), is publicly available. This model offers several advancements over existing alternative stochastic weather generators, including the ability to simulate any terrestrial region of the planet, moving from simulating a single site to an entire gridded domain and increasing the temporal resolution of temperature simulation from daily to hourly. EGGS-WG is designed to be as low resource and portable as possible, ensuring ease of use for any potential end user. This paper describes in detail all of the principles that are used in the model design and code implementation. Preliminary tests are performed over five climatically distinct regions to confirm the ability of the model to reproduce the behavior of the ERA5-Land dataset. Precipitation occurrence rates and daily rainfall amounts are shown to be reproduced accurately by the model with a range of attributes investigated, including seasonality, spatial correlations and rainfall spells. However, some clear issues remain in the simulation of the most extreme precipitation values. Similar analysis is also performed for the air temperature and dew point temperature, showing stronger agreement than the precipitation data. EGGS-WG is designed with a focus on potential future developments, including support for CMIP6 driven future warming and expansion into simulating other variables provided by the ERA5-Land dataset.

articles.title: SWORD-CTRIP mapping (SCM v1.0): a confidence-aware framework for mapping satellite-derived river reaches to gridded routing networks
articles.titleEn: SWORD-CTRIP mapping (SCM v1.0): a confidence-aware framework for mapping satellite-derived river reaches to gridded routing networks
articles.abstract: The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission provides reach-scale river observations referenced to the vector-based SWORD database. Linking these observations to gridded routing models such as CTRIP requires reconciling differences in river network representation. We present SCM v1.0, a global mapping framework that combines spatial intersection and MERIT Hydro-derived River information with a geometric scoring procedure based on proximity, reach length, and flow-direction alignment. Upstream-area mismatch is retained as a diagnostic and is not included in the weighted composite score. Single-reach cases are assigned directly, while multi-reach cases are resolved through minimum-score selection and classified using nominal High, Medium, and Low score thresholds. The archived classification convention is inconsistent with the score-minimization criterion; therefore, these labels should not be interpreted as calibrated assignment reliability. At 1/12° resolution, the final classified population comprises 123 998 CTRIP pixels, including 99 174 single-reach and 24 824 scored assignments. A MERIT-derived basin-hash diagnostic provides a qualitative check of basin-scale spatial organization but does not independently validate network connectivity. The resulting mapping products offer a reproducible basis for linking SWOT observations to CTRIP, while evaluation of network-level consistency and data-assimilation performance remains future work.

articles.title: To tip or not to tip
articles.titleEn: To tip or not to tip
articles.abstract: Tipping points have become a buzzword in Earth sciences, but ambiguous or overly narrow definitions of tipping are causing confusion around the concept. Agreeing on what tipping means, and whether a system tips or not, is important for robust science and communicating tipping risk. Based on a critical evaluation of existing tipping definitions, we propose a revised, general definition that characterizes a tipping event as a persistent nonlinear transition in forced systems. Our definition emphasizes both the phenomenology (observed time series) and cause (feedback mechanism) of a tipping event. Inspired by response theory, our proposition is compatible with more specific mathematical formulations while avoiding challenging notions such as bifurcations, equilibrium states, abruptness and irreversibility – making the definition testable also on transient dynamics in diverse complex systems under time-varying forcing. We showcase its practical use and limitations in a toy model and a case study of Earth system model data.

articles.title: Mapping 20-years winter wheat dynamics in global primary planting areas using Gaussian mixture models with adaptive thresholds
articles.titleEn: Mapping 20-years winter wheat dynamics in global primary planting areas using Gaussian mixture models with adaptive thresholds
articles.abstract: Understanding the spatiotemporal dynamics of winter wheat is essential for ensuring global food security. Currently, limited research has focused on the global dynamics of wheat over the past decades. In this study, we propose a novel framework to map fractional winter wheat dynamics from 2001 to 2020 at 1 km resolution in key global planting areas from MODIS satellite data, utilizing a flexible Gaussian mixture model (GMM). We first created the stratified samples of winter wheat fractions at 1 km resolution from multiple public crop datasets to establish the training base, and then developed a robust random forest regression model using MODIS surface reflectance to map regional fractional distributions of winter wheat. Subsequently, we estimated the actual wheat cover fractions across different regions and years by analyzing crop mixtures within 1 ° × 1 ° grids with GMM. The model parameters were utilized to determine optimal thresholds for winter wheat extraction. The performance of our proposed framework was evaluated spatially and temporally, revealing significant insights into global winter wheat dynamics. Results demonstrated that our mapping approach aligns closely with existing local winter wheat maps and statistical data, achieving annual coefficients of determination ( R 2 ) above 0.81 with FAO statistics in primary planting regions and exceeding 0.72 at subnational scales. We present the first comprehensive effort to map global winter wheat distribution and dynamics from 2001 to 2020 at a near-global scale. The proposed framework is readily adaptable to other major crops and demonstrates strong agreement with existing maps and statistical records. The resulting high-resolution global winter wheat map series provides valuable inputs for global crop modelling and contributes to achieving the “Zero Hunger”. The product is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32149033 (Wen et al., 2026).

articles.title: PhaFoS: a global database of Phanerozoic foraminiferal size
articles.titleEn: PhaFoS: a global database of Phanerozoic foraminiferal size
articles.abstract: Body size is a key phenotypic trait of living organisms, reflecting ecological function and individual metabolism. Evolutionary changes in body size also provide information on interactions between the organisms and their changing physical and biotic environments. Despite the utilitarian value of body size for understanding evolution and past environments, we lack a standardized, occurrence-based, Phanerozoic body size database for most groups of organisms, limiting large-scale studies of size evolution and size-environment interactions. Foraminifera are an ideal group to fill this data gap, given their abundant fossil record, extensive palaeogeographic distribution, and sensitivity to environmental changes. Here, we present PhaFoS, short for Pha nerozoic Fo raminifera S ize database. PhaFoS compiles 118 885 specimens, of which 103 121 from 963 published papers and the remaining 15 764 from our field colletions, representing 4167 genera and 34 256 species. Each record is linked to standardized and queryable metadata fields, including test volume (log 10 µm 3 ), taxonomy, stratigraphic age, and both modern and paleogeographic coordinates. This database can be used to quantify temporal and spatial patterns of foraminiferal body-size over the Phanerozoic, and to explore the body size relationships with environmental conditions and their changes. The data files described in this paper are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20777319 (Feng and Song, 2026).

articles.title: Modelling N 2 O emissions in fertilized grasslands with machine learning: a multi-site LSTM approach
articles.titleEn: Modelling N 2 O emissions in fertilized grasslands with machine learning: a multi-site LSTM approach
articles.abstract: Accurate quantification of GHG emissions from agricultural soils based on key environmental and management factors, is crucial for developing effective mitigation strategies. This study applies a machine learning approach using data from multiple montane grasslands in central Europe to model the spatial and temporal dynamics of N 2 O emissions, using meteorological, soil, and management data. The primary aim is to advance predictive modelling of N 2 O emissions from grassland soils for spatial upscaling and scenario analysis. Specifically, we assess whether a regionally trained model can accurately estimate N 2 O emissions from an independent site excluded from training. We collected data from five fertilized grasslands across southern Germany, northern Switzerland and western Austria (122 soil-site-treatment-year combinations), and trained a long short-term memory (LSTM) algorithm to model the influence of drivers within 5 subsequent days on N 2 O emissions. The dataset includes daily N 2 O emission measurements along with key emission drivers such as soil moisture and temperature in 10 cm soil depth, daily precipitation, occurrence of fertilization events (zero or one flag), as well as static soil characteristics such as pH and bulk density. The trained LSTM model showed varying predictive performance when evaluated on two test datasets, with higher performance at some site-years and lower at others. One test set included temporally independent data (hold-out years) (RMSE = 28 µg N 2 O-N m −2 h −1 ), while the other included cross-site data from a soil type withheld from training (RMSE = 11 µg N 2 O-N m −2 h −1 ). The model captured N 2 O dynamics, including the magnitude and timing of emission peaks driven by slurry application and environmental factors, though predictive performance varied across individual site-years. These results demonstrate that LSTM-based models can predict N 2 O emissions for most site-years across test sites with similar environmental and soil characteristics, representing an alternative to process-based models for predicting soil N 2 O emissions.

articles.title: Development of a national-scale rip current forecast for Aotearoa New Zealand
articles.titleEn: Development of a national-scale rip current forecast for Aotearoa New Zealand
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Rip currents are dangerous flows in the surfzone of wave-exposed beaches and can take bathers from the shallows into deeper water. They cause hundreds of drownings globally each year and are the leading cause of all beach lifeguard rescues. In New Zealand, with a population of approx. 5 million people, rip currents typically cause 500–1000 lifeguard rescues each year and are attributed to 53 % of all Surf Life Saving New Zealand rescues. This study aims to identify environmental conditions associated with rip current incidents and develop a simple algorithm for forecasting rip current risk and hazard. A dataset of ∼ 9000 recorded rip current rescues along with water user head counts made at 58 beaches by lifeguards around the coast of New Zealand between 2001 and 2022 was used to assess rip current risk (parameterised from the total number of incidents) and rip current hazard (parameterised as the likelihood of an individual being in a rip incident) under different wave, tide, and wind conditions. In concurrence with previous findings, most rip incidents in New Zealand were recorded at beaches with intermediate “bar-rip” beach morphology and occurred disproportionately during wave conditions at or above average breaker height with tide level at or below average low tide for a given beach. Although rip incidents were also recorded at dissipative and reflective beaches lacking in bar-rip morphology, water users were 4 and 24 times more likely, respectively, to be in a rip-related incident at intermediate beaches with bar-rip morphology. A simple, threshold-based algorithm was developed using only breaker height, relative tide level, and a binary bar-rip morphology variable as predictors for use as a national-scale rip forecast across New Zealand. The algorithm achieves a high incident hit rate, capturing 98 % of historic rip incidents across New Zealand, and captures exponentially increasing hazard at each of its five Rip Index levels, with a water user 6 times more likely to be in a rip incident at the highest Rip Index (∼ 1-in-200) compared to the lowest (∼ 1-in-1200). It also conservatively replicates a lifeguard's perception of rip hazard, with an overall agreement rate of approximately 81 %, indicating it could provide useful forewarnings to the public especially at non-lifeguarded beaches or outside lifeguard patrol hours. To our knowledge, this represents the longest running rip incident data set analysed, and most widely validated rip forecast in the literature to date.

articles.title: Co-production of knowledge for effective flood risk management
articles.titleEn: Co-production of knowledge for effective flood risk management
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Flood risks (FR) represent one of the most pressing global challenges, exacerbated by factors such as climate change, urbanization, and land use changes. Effective flood risk management (FRM) faces significant challenges, including the need for robust decision-making, the need to address existing risks, and the need to implement strategies across the disaster risk reduction (DRR) cycle. Transdisciplinary research (TD) research is expected to address complex problems by enabling processes of mutual learning in which knowledge is co-produced between science and society, integrating various knowledge claims to solve societal or real-world problems. This study makes use of TD concepts and methods and specifies them for flood risk research. It connects three conceptual perspectives: First, we identify flood-risk-specific characteristics and their implications for the design of TD research, tools, and methods. Second, we adapt the framework for impact generation in TD research (Schneider et al., 2019) by focussing on a set of generic mechanisms (i.e., knowledge production, social learning, and competence building). And third, we consider these mechanisms for generating impact as embedded in mediating processes along the flood risk research (i.e., developing joint research questions and design, building trust and creating ownership, and the institutional anchoring of results). These conceptual perspectives are used for analysing and reflecting empirical experiences from the PARADeS project in Ghana, a project that aimed for participatory flood risk reduction. The study produces in-depth insights in a transdisciplinary flood risk research project and offers conceptually and empirically grounded applications of flood-risk specific transdisciplinary methods and tools. In doing so, the study demonstrates that flood risk research requires collaborative, adaptive, and context-sensitive approaches, employing purposefully a range of methods and tools capable of integrating multiple forms of knowledge and supporting interaction across disciplines, institutions, and various stakeholder groups. The findings underline that effective flood risk management cannot rely solely on technical expertise or isolated scientific outputs. Rather, it requires reflexive and participatory processes that explicitly engage with questions of power, governance, vulnerability, and epistemic diversity. Further, the study shows that particularly in North–South collaborations, equitable partnerships and sensitivity to local contexts are crucial for generating socially robust and actionable knowledge. Finally, the study concludes that the transformative potential of flood risk research lies not only in producing better knowledge about floods, but in fostering inclusive processes of co-learning, shared ownership, and long-term institutional engagement.

articles.title: Seasonal Asynchrony of Microbial Biomass and Respiration Across Terrestrial Ecosystems
articles.titleEn: Seasonal Asynchrony of Microbial Biomass and Respiration Across Terrestrial Ecosystems
articles.abstract: Soil microorganisms are fundamental drivers of terrestrial carbon cycling, acting both as a major reservoir of carbon through their biomass and as a dominant flux via respiration. While conventional models assume a positive correlation between microbial biomass and respiration at the interannual scale, the seasonal synchrony between these two components remains poorly understood. Here, we analyzed seasonal data from 323 studies to assess the synchrony between microbial biomass carbon and respiration, and used site‐level observations to explore the underlying mechanisms. We observed a seasonal asynchrony between microbial biomass and respiration, meaning that periods of higher biomass did not consistently coincide with higher respiration rates. This seasonal asynchrony was consistent with divergent governing mechanisms, in which microbial biomass was associated with plant competition, whereas microbial respiration was closely associated with temperature. Our findings provide correlative evidence to refine microbial‐mediated carbon seasonal dynamics in Earth system models under increasing climatic seasonality.

articles.title: Unraveling the Controls of Soil Moisture and Atmospheric Water Demand on Critical Soil Moisture Variability Across Indian Biomes
articles.titleEn: Unraveling the Controls of Soil Moisture and Atmospheric Water Demand on Critical Soil Moisture Variability Across Indian Biomes
articles.abstract: The critical soil moisture (CSM) threshold marks the transition from energy‐to water‐limited vegetation functioning, constraining photosynthesis and evapotranspiration. Although often treated as a fixed ecosystem property, its sensitivity to vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and soil moisture (SM) during drydowns remains poorly understood. Shifting from high‐to low‐VPD drydowns across India redistributes land‐atmosphere coupling: ∼24.8% of grids shift from transitional (Regime 2) to transitional‐to‐wet (Regime 4), especially in the northwest, west‐central, northeast, and Western Ghats. In contrast, low‐SM drydowns shift ∼35.2% toward transitional regimes across the Indo‐Gangetic Plains, Deccan Plateau, and central‐eastern India, showing that high VPD and low SM independently affect water limitation. Biome‐specific analyses demonstrate that CSM is a dynamic rather than a stationary property of the plant‐soil continuum. High VPD produces the largest CSM reductions in deciduous forests mosaic pixels (−11.23 ± 0.36 kg m −2 ), whereas low SM has the strongest effect in savannas mosaic pixels (−14.05 ± 0.31 kg m −2 ). By explicitly separating SM and VPD coupling, we show that SM dominates CSM variability, with VPD mainly acting through its interaction with SM, as evident in croplands and grasslands. In terms of days spent in a water‐limited regime, ecosystems such as croplands, grasslands, and savanna mosaics are particularly vulnerable to compound high‐VPD and low‐SM conditions, whereas evergreen forests are comparatively resilient to atmospheric demand but highly sensitive to SM depletion. Together, these findings demonstrate the non‐stationary nature of CSM and biome‐specific vulnerabilities to intensifying hydroclimatic extremes under climate change.
articles.abstractEn: The critical soil moisture (CSM) threshold marks the transition from energy‐to water‐limited vegetation functioning, constraining photosynthesis and evapotranspiration. Shifting from high‐to low‐VPD drydowns across India redistributes land‐atmosphere coupling: ∼24.8% of grids shift from transitional (Regime 2) to transitional‐to‐wet (Regime 4), especially in the northwest, west‐central, northeast, and Western Ghats. In contrast, low‐SM drydowns shift ∼35.2% toward transitional regimes across the Indo‐Gangetic Plains, Deccan Plateau, and central‐eastern India, showing that high VPD and low SM independently affect water limitation. Biome‐specific analyses demonstrate that CSM is a dynamic rather than a stationary property of the plant‐soil continuum. High VPD produces the largest CSM reductions in deciduous forests mosaic pixels (−11.23 ± 0.36 kg m −2 ), whereas low SM has the strongest effect in savannas mosaic pixels (−14.05 ± 0.31 kg m −2 ). By explicitly separating SM and VPD coupling, we show that SM dominates CSM variability, with VPD mainly acting through its interaction with SM, as evident in croplands and grasslands. In terms of days spent in a water‐limited regime, ecosystems such as croplands, grasslands, and savanna mosaics are particularly vulnerable to compound high‐VPD and low‐SM conditions, whereas evergreen forests are comparatively resilient to atmospheric demand but highly sensitive to SM depletion. Together, these findings demonstrate the non‐stationary nature of CSM and biome‐specific vulnerabilities to intensifying hydroclimatic extremes under climate change.

articles.title: Interfacial Response of Bacterial Community Vertical Shifts in the Ice‐Water‐Sediment Vertical Sedimentary Chain of Frozen Lake Dali
articles.titleEn: Interfacial Response of Bacterial Community Vertical Shifts in the Ice‐Water‐Sediment Vertical Sedimentary Chain of Frozen Lake Dali
articles.abstract: High‐latitude lakes are ecologically important, particularly during ice‐covered periods, when three distinct media (ice, water, and sediment) and two critical interfaces, the ice‐water interface (IWI) and sediment‐water interface (SWI), are formed. Using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing, we investigated the structural characteristics of bacterial communities across these media and interfaces in Lake Dali, northern China. Along the ice‐water‐sediment chain, the relative abundances of Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Chloroflexi varied vertically with changes in phosphorus, NH 4 + ‐N, and pH, and these groups predominated in ice, water, and sediment, respectively. Network properties differed markedly among media. Water samples exhibited higher modularity and lower network density than ice and sediment samples. The operational taxonomic units associated with ecological network stability also differed between IWI and SWI. These findings suggest that environmental conditions and medium properties influence the importance of ecological network nodes, whereas relative abundance alone does not necessarily determine their importance. In ice and sediment, the solid‐state properties of the media reduced mass transfer efficiency and increased environmental isolation among communities. Consequently, stochastic processes dominated community assembly, with drift accounting for more than 30%, although heterogeneous selection also contributed substantially. In contrast, the fluidity of water increased the contribution of deterministic processes. In the water column, homogeneous selection dominated bacterial community assembly and facilitated microbial dispersal between communities. This study sheds light on the distinctive environmental distribution patterns, ecological interactions, and community assembly mechanisms of bacterial communities in frozen lakes, thereby enhancing our understanding of microbial ecological processes across ice‐water‐sediment interfaces.

articles.title: Leveraging High‐Resolution Topobathymetry to Assess Parsimonious Reach‐Scale Flood Inundation Mapping
articles.titleEn: Leveraging High‐Resolution Topobathymetry to Assess Parsimonious Reach‐Scale Flood Inundation Mapping
articles.abstract: Forecasting flood inundation requires accurate flood discharges, topography, and a means to map discharge to water level. In the continental United States, the National Water Model forecasts flooded areas using the Height Above Nearest Drainage—Flood Inundation Mapping (HAND‐FIM) approach. HAND‐FIM utilizes a Synthetic Rating Curve (SRC) and forecasted discharge to compute flood inundation within a river reach. Within the National Water Model, SRCs are currently developed using river segment‐averaged geometry extracted from a 10‐m Digital Elevation Model; however, high‐resolution topography and hydrodynamic models allow the full complexity of channel morphology to be leveraged to assess the HAND‐FIM approach. We utilize high‐resolution topobathymetry coupled with satellite images across a range of flows and established rating curves to calibrate 2D hydraulic models for three reaches of the South Fork Eel River, California. To assess the impact of reach‐scale hydraulic variability on SRCs, we construct an ensemble of rating curves based on high‐resolution cross‐stream elevation transects. We generate inundation extents using the ensemble of rating curves and HAND‐SRCs and assess their performance against the calibrated model inundation extents. We find that a single rating curve can produce accurate reach‐scale flood inundation, although it is not the rating curve that best represents reach‐scale hydraulics. HAND‐FIM performance improves when slope, roughness, and channel geometry within the SRC are corrected together, as correcting parameters individually can reduce performance. Improving the HAND‐FIM approach has the potential to reduce uncertainty in flood prediction and provide advanced warning of flood extent across the United States.

articles.title: Data Assimilation to Inform Strategic Network Placement and Evaluate the Added Value of the Next Generation Water Observing System for Hydrologic Modeling and Prediction
articles.titleEn: Data Assimilation to Inform Strategic Network Placement and Evaluate the Added Value of the Next Generation Water Observing System for Hydrologic Modeling and Prediction
articles.abstract: Streamflow observations play a critical role in hydrologic modeling, supporting a wide range of applications. Although increasing the density of streamflow measurements is desirable, the installation and maintenance of new streamgauges can be time intensive and cost prohibitive. Strategic placement of new observation sites is desired both in terms of cost associated with their operation, and also the desire to make the benefits of the observation optimal for its applications. This study explores the application of observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs) to guide the placement of streamgauges within the Delaware River Basin. The results show that OSSEs can help guide selection of candidate locations for new streamgauges within an existing observing network. This study also assesses the impact of existing U.S. Geological Survey streamgauges, particularly those deployed as part of the Next Generation Water Observing System (NGWOS) in improving hydrologic model performance through data assimilation (DA). The HydroDART framework that couples the Weather Research and Forecasting Hydrological modeling system (WRF‐Hydro) with the Data Assimilation Research Testbed (DART) is used here to evaluate the impact of these gauges. Findings indicate that applying DA using non‐NGWOS gauges improves the median Kling‐Gupta efficiency (KGE) from 0.42 to 0.71 for high‐flow events. Inclusion of NGWOS gauges further increases the median KGE value to 0.76. Using advanced data assimilation methods such as the hybrid ensemble Kalman filter‐optimal interpolation (EnKF‐OI) substantially improves the prediction skill emphasizing the importance of blending in climatological information, in addition to the flow‐dependent ensemble, to make the most of available observations.

articles.title: Inflow and Infiltration Localization for Urban Sewer Networks Using Point of Interest‐Based Hydraulic Model and Pipe Infiltration Likelihood Model
articles.titleEn: Inflow and Infiltration Localization for Urban Sewer Networks Using Point of Interest‐Based Hydraulic Model and Pipe Infiltration Likelihood Model
articles.abstract: Inflow and infiltration (I&I) is a typical issue in separated urban sewer networks (USNs) contributing to treatment plants overloads, combined sewer overflows, urban flooding and other environmental problems. However, the lack of spatio‐temporal inflow data from real‐time monitoring and field measurements presents a challenge in accurately identifying I&I locations. To address this, this study proposes a novel I&I localization method based on Point of Interest (POI)‐based hydraulic model and pipe infiltration likelihood model (PILM), with open‐source public databases. Sewer inflows for each manhole are estimated based on connected building discharges from surrounding areas derived from building type and area information obtained from POI database. An optimization approach based on Iterative Local Updating Ensemble Smoother is employed to calibrate a USN dry‐weather hydraulic model, determining time‐series inflows by using the previously estimated flows as prior information. The calibrated hydraulic model is further integrated with the PILM to estimate and localize I&I flows within the network. The proposed method is applied to a real USN in southern China. Results demonstrate good agreement between simulated and observed sewer flows and water depths under dry‐weather conditions, with mean KGE and R 2 values both of 0.94 at flow monitoring locations and 0.92 and 0.86 for the water level monitoring locations. Estimated I&I flows achieve average KGE and R 2 values of 0.79 and 0.82. Field sampling confirms the reliability of the I&I localization results. The proposed I&I estimation and localization method has the potential to enhance USN management and inform related maintenance and rehabilitation efforts.

articles.title: Near‐Term Anthropogenic Aerosol Reductions Under a Future Sustainability Pathway Could Avoid Nearly 40% of Mid‐Century PM 2.5 Mortality
articles.titleEn: Near‐Term Anthropogenic Aerosol Reductions Under a Future Sustainability Pathway Could Avoid Nearly 40% of Mid‐Century PM 2.5 Mortality
articles.abstract: Ambitious climate and air quality mitigation cuts anthropogenic aerosol emissions, lowering fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) and mortality, but the magnitude, regional distribution, and uncertainty of these reductions remain insufficiently quantified. Using nine Earth System Models from the Regional Aerosol Model Intercomparison Project (RAMIP), we quantify the PM 2.5 mortality benefits of switching anthropogenic aerosols alone from a low mitigation (SSP3‐7.0) to a high mitigation (SSP1‐2.6) scenario. The switch avoids 2.36 million (95% CI: 1.48–2.57 million) deaths/year globally in 2050, equivalent to 38% of SSP3‐7.0 PM 2.5 ‐attributable mortality. Benefits are largest in East Asia, South Asia, and Africa and smaller in North America and Europe. Global land annual mean PM 2.5 falls by 2%–17% across the RAMIP experiments, reaching 33%–38% near Asian sources. Cuts in East Asia alone avoid 48% of source region and 22% of global PM 2.5 mortality. Uncertainty is dominated by inter‐model variability, followed by health response functions and natural climate variability. Overall, sustainability‐pathway aerosol reductions can avoid nearly 40% of projected PM 2.5 deaths by 2050, with health benefits that are large but highly unevenly spatially distributed.

articles.title: City‐Wide Impacts of Cooling Infrastructure on Urban Outdoor Heat Stress of Populations With Diverse Physiological Characteristics
articles.titleEn: City‐Wide Impacts of Cooling Infrastructure on Urban Outdoor Heat Stress of Populations With Diverse Physiological Characteristics
articles.abstract: Adaptation strategies to reduce urban overheating are necessary to counteract rising trends in population exposure to extreme heat and associated health issues. The impact of these strategies has been traditionally assessed using only surface or air temperature ( T a ), but some of these strategies may involve trade‐offs and need to be evaluated using more comprehensive metrics. In this study, we combine a physiologically‐based human heat balance model with a mesoscale meteorological model developed for outdoor thermal exposure to assess the impacts of street trees and cool (reflective) roofs, walls and pavement on heat stress across diverse populations. The study focuses on the hot and arid Las Vegas Valley and considers five representative personal profiles that combine different physical and behavioral characteristics. All strategies reduce daytime T a , but radiation effects dominate, leading to contrasting impacts on human heat stress across metrics. Street trees produce the smallest T a reductions but the largest heat stress benefit due to shade provision. In contrast, reflective walls and pavements increase heat stress by reflecting radiation toward pedestrians, even though they produce larger T a reductions. Under the assumption of continuous outdoor exposure, we find large differences across population groups, with the more sensitive profiles experiencing over twice as many hours of uncompensable heat stress relative to young individuals. Our results highlight the importance of considering context‐specific profiles and examining the different avenues of heat exchange on humans when assessing the impacts of cooling strategies on urban overheating and heat stress.

articles.title: Assessing Future Agricultural Flood Risks in China Under Climate Change: Shifting Peaks and Land‐Use Feedback
articles.titleEn: Assessing Future Agricultural Flood Risks in China Under Climate Change: Shifting Peaks and Land‐Use Feedback
articles.abstract: The complex interplay between climate‐driven flood hazards and evolving cropland patterns poses a critical threat to food security. Prevailing assessments frequently treat these elements in isolation, overlooking the spatiotemporal feedbacks arising from their dynamic co‐evolution. We developed a multi‐factor simulation framework integrating various emission scenarios (RCP4.5 and RCP8.5), projected cropland dynamics, and growth‐stage‐specific flood sensitivity for rice, wheat, and maize. Taking China as a typical case, results reveal a seasonal shift in peak flood losses from July–August to May–June under the adopted modeling framework. This peak shift creates a phenological mismatch that intensifies threats during vulnerable crop growth stages. Compared to RCP4.5, the loss patterns under RCP8.5 exhibit a distinct northward expansion into higher latitudes. Under the RCP4.5 scenario, annual losses are projected to escalate significantly, increasing by approximately 9% by 2050 and over 40% by 2080 relative to the baseline. In contrast, RCP8.5 drives a near‐term increase (36% by 2050) followed by a decline to approximately 32% above baseline by 2080, as substantial cropland contraction partially offsets the intensifying climate hazards. The RCP8.5 losses remain approximately 11%–12% below RCP4.5 losses by 2080, reflecting the combined effect of intensified hazard and reduced exposure rather than a convergence to equivalent risk. This study highlights that long‐term flood risk emerges from the co‐evolution of climate hazards and land use, offering critical scientific support for tailored flood prevention and climate adaptation strategies in China.

articles.title: From Precipitation Deficits to Agricultural Stress: Timescale‐Dependent Drought Response in China's Main Grain Region
articles.titleEn: From Precipitation Deficits to Agricultural Stress: Timescale‐Dependent Drought Response in China's Main Grain Region
articles.abstract: Understanding the response of agricultural drought to meteorological drought across multi‐timescales is crucial for drought monitoring and management. However, both the timescale dependence and regional heterogeneity of this linkage have yet to be adequately clarified. Focusing on China's main grain region, we explored the spatiotemporal variability of meteorological drought and its time‐lagged influence on agricultural drought at monthly, seasonal, annual, and interannual timescales. Meteorological drought was represented by precipitation anomaly (PA), and agricultural drought was captured by leaf area index anomaly. Using a multi‐timescale framework that integrated the estimates of lag time, correlation strength and drought response intensity, we mapped where and at what scales rainfall deficits translate into vegetation stress. Results indicated a clear north‐south gradient pattern in PA variability, with distinct spatial distributions across timescales. Meteorological drought propagated to agricultural drought in a timescale‐dependent manner, with lag times increasing from 32.8 to 1031.3 days and PA–LAIA correlations strengthening from 0.13 to 0.48 as timescale expand. However, significant PA–LAIA linkages were stronger and covered broader areas at monthly (∼64%) and interannual (∼76.1%) timescales, suggesting widespread vegetation responses to rainfall deficits. They were further classified into three response levels by considering the impact of aridity index. Weak response areas, largely influenced by low temperature, are located in southern and eastern parts of Northeast China and the Inner Mongolia Region (NEC‐IMR). Moderate and strong responses occur in northern NEC‐IMR and southern Yangtze River Basin at monthly timescale, and in northern NEC‐IMR and central Huang‐Huai‐Hai Region at interannual timescale. These findings highlight the timescale‐dependent regulation of drought responses, with implications for guiding drought mitigation and water management.

articles.title: Disentangling the Spread in Wind Projections Over Europe and the Impacts on Energy Generation
articles.titleEn: Disentangling the Spread in Wind Projections Over Europe and the Impacts on Energy Generation
articles.abstract: Future changes in near‐surface wind speed currently display a large spread and uncertainty. A better understanding of future wind projections will enable the anticipation and enhancement of clean energy generation. Here, we provide insights on model spread over Europe employing a large ensemble of sub‐daily bias‐adjusted CMIP6 wind simulations, for the historical (1979–2014) and future (2041–2100) periods under different socio‐economic scenarios. Europe is projected to experience a gradual weakening of near‐surface wind speed, especially over central and southern regions during winter, and a strengthening in northern Europe and southern latitudes during summer. These changes typically intensify and become more spatially coherent by the late 21st century in the worst‐case scenario (SSP585). Climate change may modestly enhance wind capacity factor (WCF) for energy generation in southern Europe (Iberia) during summer, while generally decreasing in the rest of Europe. During winter, WCF remains relatively stable (with decreases in Eastern Europe and northern latitudes) but is affected by larger uncertainty. Based on hierarchical clustering, sub‐ensembles of models are constructed, showing differences not only in the magnitude and sign of WCF changes, but also in their regional heterogeneity. We show that uncertainty in wind speed and wind energy production is strongly shaped by model and scenario differences, and reinforce the need to account for the diurnal cycle and seasonal differences at a regional scale. Furthermore, strengthened NAO‐WCF coupling and more positive mean NAO states may enhance northern European wind resources, while reduced variance could diminish year‐to‐year variability, important for long‐term energy planning.

articles.title: Beyond Extremes: Asymmetric Coupling Strength and Sensitivity of Global Vegetation Productivity to Precipitation
articles.titleEn: Beyond Extremes: Asymmetric Coupling Strength and Sensitivity of Global Vegetation Productivity to Precipitation
articles.abstract: Precipitation is a primary driver of terrestrial vegetation productivity, and their coupling reflects key carbon‐water interactions in ecosystems. While asymmetric productivity responses to extreme precipitation anomalies are recognized, it remains unknown whether fundamental ecosystem indicators like coupling strength (the correlation between productivity and precipitation) and response sensitivity (the regression slope) are also asymmetric under non‐extreme conditions. Here, using multi‐source remote sensing proxies and precipitation records, we constructed three asymmetric indices based on extreme values, coupling strength (correlation coefficients), and sensitivity (regression slopes) to systematically evaluate their global spatiotemporal patterns. We found that 41.4% of global vegetated areas exhibit significant asymmetry (with 19.4% remaining robustly asymmetric even after strictly filtering out the impact of observation noise). Although negative asymmetry generally dominates (∼70% overall, and >80% within the strictly noise‐filtered domain), striking divergences in both direction and magnitude emerge among the indices. Over the past four decades, ∼12% of vegetated lands (predominantly grasslands) exhibited a shift toward greater symmetry, driven by disproportionately enhanced vegetation sensitivity during wet years. These findings redefine our understanding of non‐linear vegetation‐precipitation interactions, providing critical insights for land managers to optimize drought mitigation and for climate modelers to refine carbon sequestration projections.

articles.title: Policy‐Guided Interregional Agricultural Cooperation Alters Water‐Energy‐Food Trade‐Offs in Cascade Reservoir Systems Under Climate Change
articles.titleEn: Policy‐Guided Interregional Agricultural Cooperation Alters Water‐Energy‐Food Trade‐Offs in Cascade Reservoir Systems Under Climate Change
articles.abstract: Climate change is altering precipitation, temperature, runoff, and crop water requirements, thereby changing both the availability and timing of water for irrigation and hydropower. In river basins regulated by multiple reservoirs, these changes can intensify competition between the two sectors, which depend on the same finite and seasonally variable water resources. Coordinated regional agricultural policies can shift irrigation water demand and thereby affect reservoir operation and water‐energy‐food trade‐offs. This study develops a policy‐to‐operation framework that represents regional cooperation through combinations of agricultural‐support levels and traces how the resulting demand changes affect WEF trade‐offs through the joint operation of cascade reservoirs. The framework is applied to the Upper Yellow River Basin and its 23‐reservoir system. Six agricultural support levels are assigned to each of four policy regions, resulting in 1,296 policy combinations evaluated under three CMIP6 SSPs in the near and far future. Raising agricultural support from the lowest to the highest level increases irrigation demand by approximately 37.1%, while reducing hydropower generation by 0.26%–1.15% and irrigation supply reliability by 2.15–4.89 percentage points in the near future. Policy effects are regionally asymmetric, with Gansu and Ningxia exerting the strongest influence on reservoir system outcomes. Nevertheless, 19.14%–37.58% of the configurations improve hydropower generation and irrigation supply reliability while reducing spill relative to the uniform medium support baseline, indicating that differentiated regional coordination can mitigate these conflicts. Preferred configurations vary across scenarios and periods, supporting differentiated and adaptive regional cooperation under climate change.

articles.title: Mitigating Non‐Stationarity in Machine Learning–Based Downscaling of Climate Projections
articles.titleEn: Mitigating Non‐Stationarity in Machine Learning–Based Downscaling of Climate Projections
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models perform well for climate downscaling when training and testing data follow similar statistical distributions. However, their performance can degrade as future climate statistics depart from the historical training record. We systematically investigate this problem by downscaling global temperature and precipitation fields across multiple emission pathways and two solar radiation modification (SRM) scenarios in the Max Planck Institute Earth System Model, comparing four machine learning configurations with bilinear interpolation and quantile delta mapping (QDM). A baseline ML model trained on the historical period degrades substantially under future forcing, reaching a global mean temperature error of 1.6C by 2100 under SSP5‐8.5. Preprocessing the ML model's input and target to reduce non‐stationarity via detrending and residual correction keeps the global mean error within 0.2C, comparable to that of QDM. All downscaling methods compared here show substantially lower skill when evaluated on anomalies rather than total fields, suggesting that much of their skill comes from correcting the climatological mean. QDM better preserves precipitation extremes and fine‐scale variance, whereas the ML models have lower pointwise errors. Downscaling the SRM scenarios produces larger spatial temperature biases than the emission pathways. We also generate 0.25 monthly temperature projections for G6sulfur, providing a benchmark for future regional downscaling studies.

articles.title: Resolution Controls on SST–Precipitation Coupling in Western Boundary Currents
articles.titleEn: Resolution Controls on SST–Precipitation Coupling in Western Boundary Currents
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Western boundary currents (WBCs) are hotspots of air–sea interaction where observations show strong local covariability between sea surface temperature (SST) and precipitation anomalies. We investigate how oceanic and atmospheric horizontal resolution, mesoscale SST variability, and the treatment of atmospheric convection control this coupling across the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Agulhas, and Brazil currents. Using a coordinated hierarchy of ICON and EC‐Earth3P model simulations spanning horizontal resolutions of about 5–100 km, either parameterizing or explicitly simulating atmospheric convection, complementary atmosphere‐only sensitivity experiments forced with mesoscale‐resolving or smoothed SSTs, and the CMIP6 ensemble, we assess how model design impacts the strength and spatial structure of SST–precipitation covariability. Resolving mesoscale SST variability is necessary to reproduce the observed localized precipitation responses, but a high horizontal resolution alone does not guarantee full realism. Overly broad coupling emerges in simulations with 5–25 km oceanic resolutions, while explicitly simulating atmospheric convection at 10 km atmospheric resolution produces weaker, more spatially confined precipitation responses than parameterized convection. Whereas mesoscale SST variability sets the potential for strong SST–precipitation coupling, atmospheric physics controls the efficiency of the precipitation response. Our results emphasize the importance of both increasing model resolution and improving its physics for representing realistic air–sea coupling in next‐generation climate simulations.

articles.title: Improving weather radar rainfall estimates by merging with commercial microwave link data: a fully reproducible, large-scale method intercomparison
articles.titleEn: Improving weather radar rainfall estimates by merging with commercial microwave link data: a fully reproducible, large-scale method intercomparison
articles.abstract: Accurate rainfall estimation is essential for hydrometeorological applications, but capturing the fine spatiotemporal variability of rainfall remains challenging. In this study, we assess the impact of merging commercial microwave link (CML) data with weather radar for quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) using two openly available datasets with contrasting observational densities. We compare multiple merging methods, including kriging with external drift (KED), and derive a block kriging interpolation method to account for the line-average nature of CMLs. The results show that merging CML data improves radar QPE, with reductions in mean absolute error (MAE) of up to 41 % for multiplicative merging and up to 38 % for KED, aligning well with similar studies using rain gauges. Performance depends on rainfall intensity, distance, and network density: in sparse networks, multiplicative methods yield the lowest RMSE and MAE, indicating that radar errors are dominated by scaling errors, though KED and additive methods maintain slightly higher spatial correlation (PCC) over distance. In dense networks, all methods perform comparably. Overall, additive methods perform best at capturing extremes. Despite accounting for line-averaging, block kriging performed similarly to point-based kriging. All merging methods reduced RMSE and MAE compared to unadjusted radar fields. The merging framework and intercomparison study are openly available, enabling reproducibility and further exploration by the scientific community.

articles.title: Unravelling groundwater's role in soil-plant-atmosphere continuum: integrated ecohydrological modelling approach using STEMMUS-SCOPE and MODFLOW 6
articles.titleEn: Unravelling groundwater's role in soil-plant-atmosphere continuum: integrated ecohydrological modelling approach using STEMMUS-SCOPE and MODFLOW 6
articles.abstract: Soil-plant-atmosphere continuum (SPAC) models are commonly used to investigate various components' role(s) in ecosystem functioning. Yet, in most SPAC models, groundwater is ignored or at best represented in an over-simplified manner, leading to misunderstanding of its critical role in simulating soil-vegetation dynamics. This study investigates groundwater's role in SPAC processes, in particular, the impacts of groundwater component (mass and energy) on: (1) regulating the soil profile, in terms of moisture and temperature; (2) the dynamics of the unsaturated/saturated zones and their further impact on water fluxes; and (3) the carbon fluxes and vegetation physiological processes (i.e. root water uptake and photosynthesis reflected by fluorescence). To address this, an integrated ecohydrological modelling (IEM) framework is developed by coupling the STEMMUS-SCOPE SPAC model with the MODFLOW 6 integrated hydrological model. The standalone STEMMUS-SCOPE (ST-SC) and the coupled STEMMUS-SCOPE-MODFLOW 6 (ST-SC-MF6) models were applied over an 8-year period (1 April 2016–31 March 2024) to three sites in the Netherlands (Loobos, Cabauw and Veenkampen). Various essential variables, including soil moisture ( θ ), soil temperature ( T s ), groundwater level (GWL), groundwater temperature (GT), evapotranspiration (ET), gross primary productivity (GPP), net ecosystem exchange (NEE), and sun-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) were simulated and then compared to corresponding in-situ observations. Performance of both ST-SC and ST-SC-MF6 was evaluated using the Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) and the root mean square error (RMSE) metrics. Results indicated that the groundwater contribution is spatially and temporally variable. The ST-SC-MF6 model showed better agreement with observations than the ST-SC, improving the KGE values for: (a) θ (+0.29), T s (+0.19), and ET (+0.35) at Loobos, (b) θ (+0.30), T s (+0.14), NEE (+0.18), and SIF (+0.15) at Cabauw, and (c) θ (+0.21) and ET (+0.15) at Veenkampen. Notably, benefits of ST-SC-MF6 simulation were particularly prominent during both wet and dry periods, i.e. improving the representation of: (a) the θ dynamics during wet conditions, when hydraulic connectivity between the phreatic surface and the unsaturated zone is strong; (b) the root water uptake and carbon assimilation during dry periods, when shallow groundwater mitigated vegetative water stress; and (c) the T s dynamics during both wet and dry periods, influenced by both GT and GWL, and further propagated to other T s -dependent processes/variables such as canopy temperature. Overall, the proposed ST-SC-MF6 IEM helped to: (1) incorporate groundwater as a key component of the water, energy and carbon cycles; and (2) define the important role groundwater dynamics plays in the SPAC for deepening the understanding of ecosystem functioning.
